abstract: |
  Governments that let capital and people move freely find it hard to tax mobile income at high rates, so they give up on high rates altogether. This section argues that the constraint binds only on the wrong base. Economic rent, the return above what an investor needs to stay, can be taxed heavily without driving anything away, because land cannot move and market power earned in a country's market is earned from its customers. The section's paper, Rent Tax, combines a land value tax above a household allowance with three corporate instruments that presume large firms hold market power: a high rate on profits above a normal return, a narrow destination-based tax on mobile rent-bearing sectors, and a sales tax with deductions for genuine local investment and employment. Longer and older treatments of tax and fiscal reform, including the book *Plucked!* and a note on India's legacy coal power contracts, are kept in section 8.

*Overview of section 2, version 0.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated.*

# Free movement limits the rates a country can charge on mobile income {.unnumbered}

Free movement of capital and people makes high tax rates on mobile bases hard to sustain. Across the OECD after 1970, and within the EU under the Maastricht Treaty, a country that tries to tax capital income at a high rate under an origin-based corporate tax watches the capital leave, and a country that taxes personal wealth heavily without exit controls watches the wealthy follow it. The usual response is to give up on high rates.

That response gives up more than it needs to. The rate a country can sustain depends on the base. Taxing a base that can leave invites it to leave. Taxing a base that cannot leave, or that earns its return from the country's own customers, does not. The papers in this section look for those bases and design instruments that reach them.

The section sits beside the carbon-pricing papers of section 1 rather than inside them. Carbon pricing taxes a harm; the instruments here tax rent. Both are cases of the same rule: put the tax where it changes behavior you want changed, or where it changes no behavior at all.

# Tax land above an allowance and presume that large firms earn rent (paper 2.1) {.unnumbered}

The Rent Tax paper rests on two bases that meet the test. The first is land, whose supply is fixed and whose value reflects a location the owner did not create. The second is corporate market power, whose value reflects network effects, brand, scale, regulatory protection and incumbency.

Land is taxed through a simplified reverse wealth tax. Every household receives an allowance of landholding value that is exempt; above it, the household pays a standard land value tax on the assessed site value. The allowance keeps the tax off ordinary homeowners and puts it on large holdings.

The corporate side reverses the usual presumption. Standard analysis treats market power as an exception that must be proven before it is taxed. The paper treats it as the default for firms above a size threshold, with the burden of proof on the firm, and a narrow carve-out for sectors where scale is a technical necessity, such as civil aircraft and leading-edge chip manufacturing. Three instruments follow. An allowance for corporate equity exempts the normal return and taxes the residual at a high rate. A narrow destination-based tax reaches mobile rent-bearing sectors such as digital platforms and pharmaceutical intellectual property, credited against the first layer. A simple sales tax applies to all large firms, with deductions for in-country assets and payroll, so a firm that invests and employs locally pays little while a firm that books sales without local presence pays more.

The design discriminates between rent and effort. In the paper's comparison, an asset-light multinational with large in-country sales faces a combined effective rate of 40 to 60 percent on the rent it earns from domestic customers, while a capital-intensive domestic firm pays close to nothing on its normal return. The paper sets the calculation out as a five-step algorithm that uses data large groups already report, and argues that each instrument is compatible with free-movement law; it cites the European Court of Justice's 2020 rulings upholding Hungary's turnover tax. Its rough revenue estimates for a medium-sized European economy, 5.5 to 11.5 percent of GDP, are orders of magnitude rather than forecasts.

The paper is a sketch, written in April 2026, and has not yet been revised to the series standard. It has no brief and no deck.

# Related work in section 8 {.unnumbered}

Two pieces of related fiscal work are kept with the additional papers in section 8, because they are older, longer or not yet written up.

*Plucked! A Guide to a Fair, Simple, Efficient and Politically Feasible Tax and Benefits System* (with Gordon Styles, 2020) is a book-length case for reforming UK tax and benefits. Its fourteen chapters cover tax principles and practice, welfare and work, inequality, corporations, land and property, money and debt, and environment and resources. Its chapters on land and corporations are the long form of the argument that Rent Tax states in a few pages. The manuscript is kept as written in 2020 and has not been revised (section 8.5, paper 8.5.3).

*Stranded by Contract: Reforming Legacy Coal Power Purchase Agreements* starts from the observation that a coal plant can be stranded in economic terms while its contract keeps the money flowing. Where the variable cost of coal generation exceeds the all-in cost of new solar, retiring the plant and buying solar power instead saves money before any climate benefit is counted. The folder holds India country material but no paper yet (section 8.1, paper 8.1.1).
